parts.title: TypeScript for sharing a value between tests

blocks.text:
# Week 3, Day 2.1 — TypeScript for sharing a value between tests

Two ideas are new today; a third you already have. Today one test creates something the
next test needs, and that's why the value has to survive the trip from a hook into a test.

> **Every run starts fresh.** Each time you press Run, your code starts from a clean slate. Nothing from a previous run is still in memory.

| # | Concept | Why today needs it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `let` vs `var` (`const` is a recap) | the shared page is created later, so it needs `let` |
| 2 | Block scope vs module scope | "global" variables, and why they're needed here |
| 3 | Arrow functions, including `async` ones | already covered — see [Week 1, Day 5.1](/learn/w1/d5/p1) |

## 1. `let`, `const`, `var`

You already met `const` — and dynamic typing — in
[Week 2, Day 2.1](/learn/w2/d2/p1). Today adds the other two.

| Keyword | Reassign? | Scope | Use it? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `const` | no | block | **default choice** |
| `let` | yes | block | when the value arrives later |
| `var` | yes | function — leaks out of blocks | **no** |

`var` is the old form and it ignores block boundaries, which produces bugs that look like
magic. Modern TypeScript has no reason to use it.

**Expected:** `before: ""`, then `after: "a token…"`, then both values inside the block, then
`I escaped` from outside it.

That last line is the whole case against `var`. `leaks` was declared inside an `if` and is
still readable afterwards — so two unrelated blocks can quietly share a name.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 2. Block scope vs module scope

Where you *declare* a variable decides who can see it.

- Inside `{ }` → only that block. Gone when the block ends.
- At the top of the file, outside everything → the whole file can see it. This is what people
  mean by a **global** variable.

Today's problem in one sentence: a hook creates the page, and the tests need it — two
different blocks, so the variable has to live outside both.

**Expected:** `not created yet`, then `created inside a function`, then
`readsIt sees: created inside a function`.

### The mistake this prevents

```ts
let page;                              // outside, correct

test.beforeAll(async ({ browser }) => {
  const page = await browser.newPage();   // WRONG: a second, separate variable
});
```

The inner `const page` is a brand-new variable that dies with the hook. The outer one is still
undefined, and every test then fails with `Cannot read properties of undefined`. Drop the
`const` and just assign.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 3. Arrow functions, and `async` ones

Already fully covered in
[Week 1, Day 5.1 — the TypeScript for your first real test](/learn/w1/d5/p1): the
plain form, the `async` form, and destructuring in the parameter list (`({ page }) => {}`)
— which is the exact shape every hook below uses.

If it has been a few weeks, a two-minute reread there is worth more than repeating it here.

## Recap

| Concept | Remember |
|---|---|
| `const` / `let` / `var` | `const` by default, `let` when it arrives later, never `var`. |
| Module scope | A value shared between hook and test must be declared outside both. |
| `async ({ x }) => {}` | The shape of every hook and test — see [Week 1, Day 5.1](/learn/w1/d5/p1) if this is unfamiliar. |

**Next:** [Day 2.2 — Hooks, grouping and isolation](/learn/w3/d2/p2)

# Week 3, Day 2.2 — One login, several tests

Split a long test into small ones and something surprising happens: each one starts logged
out. By the end of this lesson you'll know why, and the two different ways to fix it.

> **Try it here.** Write code in the editor on the right and press Run. Your code drives a real browser, and the results appear beside it.

## The problem

You had one long test doing login → view history → pay a bill → log out. You split it into
four, which is better practice: each failure now names one thing.

But test 2 fails. It can't find the dashboard, because **it isn't logged in**.

That's not a bug — it's Playwright's central design decision. **Every test gets a fresh,
isolated browser context**: no cookies, no storage, nothing carried over. That's what makes
tests safe to run in any order and in parallel. It also means state you *want* to keep has to
be set up deliberately.

## Example 1 — watch the isolation happen

**Objective:** log in, then prove a second context knows nothing about it.

**Expected:**

```
A: signed in           url=dashboard  "Leela" present=true
B: fresh context       url=dashboard  "Leela" present=false
A localStorage.proof: written in A
B localStorage.proof: null
```

Two separate lessons here, and the second one is a gift.

**Isolation is real.** `proof` was written in context A and context B sees `null`. Two contexts
in one browser process share nothing — which is exactly what happens between two tests.

**But look at context B's URL.** It asked for `/dashboard` and *got* the dashboard. This app has
**no route guard** — the shell renders for anyone who types the URL. What's missing is the user's
name, because there's no session behind it.

So a test asserting `toHaveURL(/dashboard/)` as proof of login would **pass while logged out**.
Assert on user-specific data instead. That's a real bug this app will let you write, and it's
worth more than the tidy redirect I expected to show you.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## `page` and `browser` are different tools

| Fixture | Scope | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `page` | **per test** | a fresh, isolated page. Nothing carried over. |
| `browser` | **per worker** | the shared browser process. You can open your own pages from it. |

So there are two ways to share a login:

- Ask for `browser` in `beforeAll`, open **one** page yourself, and let every test use it.
- Keep `page` per test and log in each time via `beforeEach`.

Neither is "correct" — they trade speed against isolation, and Day 2.3 argues about which.

## The four hooks

| Hook | Runs |
|---|---|
| `beforeAll` | once, before the first test in the group |
| `beforeEach` | before **every** test |
| `afterEach` | after every test |
| `afterAll` | once, after the last test |

`test.describe("name", () => { ... })` groups tests, and hooks apply to the group they're
declared in. Grouping is also how you run a related set together — the tests below depend on
each other, so running one alone would fail.

**Hooks are not tests.** They won't appear in the HTML report as passing tests, because they
are setup and teardown, not things being verified. Same idea as `@BeforeTest` in Selenium's
TestNG.

## Example 2 — one login, shared

**Objective:** build the shared page by hand, the way `beforeAll` does it.

**Expected:** ``` logged in once: https://test-automation-banking.vercel.app/dashboard Transaction History -> accountDashboard Pay Bills -> paymentDashboard Add Payee -> transferDashboard ``` Three journeys, one login. In a real spec the login moves into `beforeAll` and each tile becomes its own `test()`. Note the tiles are `

` elements, not links — `getByRole("link", …)` finds **nothing** on this dashboard. That's a real quirk of this app, and the reason these use `getByText`. **Challenge:** add `Manage Payee` to the list. Which URL does it open?

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Dependent tests need `workers: 1`

Sharing a page has a consequence: those tests can no longer run **at the same time**. Two
workers would drive the same page simultaneously and interfere.

Two ways to say so:

| Setting | Where | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `test.describe.configure({ mode: "serial" })` | in the spec | that group runs in order, in one worker |
| `workers: 1` | in the config | the whole suite runs single-file |
| `fullyParallel: false` | in the config | files run in parallel, tests within a file don't |

**Prefer the in-spec `serial`.** It's local to the tests that actually depend on each other,
so the rest of the suite keeps its parallelism. Setting `workers: 1` globally to fix three
dependent tests slows down every other test you own.

If dependent tests run in parallel you get failures that look random: the update runs before
the create, so it fails; rerun and the order differs, so something else fails.

await browser.close();
console.log("browser closed");
## The same thing, as a real spec

> ▶ **Run it yourself:** `npx playwright test week3/generated/day2-hooks.spec.ts`

**Expected:** `6 passed`.

Read the two halves. The first `describe` shares one page from `beforeAll` and is marked
`serial`. The second uses the plain `page` fixture, and both of its tests start **logged out** —
proving the isolation from Example 1 inside the real runner.

One detail worth keeping: `browser` is available in `beforeAll` but `page` is **not**, because
`page` is test-scoped and there's no test running yet. That constraint is the reason the shared
page has to be built by hand.

## Best practices

- **Group dependent tests** in a `describe` and mark it `serial` — not the whole suite.
- **Declare shared values with `let`, outside the hooks**, and assign inside.
- **Close what you open.** A page opened in `beforeAll` gets closed in `afterAll`.
- **Prefer independent tests.** Sharing is a tool, not a default.

## Common mistakes

| You see | Usually means | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'goto')` | `const page` inside the hook | drop the `const`, assign to the outer `let` |
| Test 2 starts logged out | that's isolation working | share via `beforeAll`, or log in per test |
| Random failures with dependent tests | running in parallel | `mode: "serial"` |
| `page` unavailable in `beforeAll` | it's test-scoped | use `browser` and open your own page |
| Hooks missing from the report | they aren't tests | correct — nothing to fix |

**Next:** [Day 2.3](/learn/w3/d2/p3) — why a shared page is a smell, and what a suite does instead.

parts.title: Shared state, and the better answer

blocks.text:
# Week 3, Day 2.3 — Shared state, and the better answer

Same hooks as [Day 2.2](/learn/w3/d2/p2). No new API. What changes is the honest assessment: the
shared-page trick works, and a real suite still avoids it.

## The cost of that shared page

| Consequence | Why it hurts |
|---|---|
| Tests must run in order | one failure cascades — steps 2, 3, 4 fail because step 1 did |
| No parallelism in the group | four dependent tests take four times as long |
| Cannot run one test alone | debugging step 3 means running 1 and 2 first |
| Order is invisible in the code | `serial` is one line; the dependency is everywhere |

That third row is the expensive one. When step 3 fails in CI at 3am you want to run *step 3*.
If it only works as part of a chain, every debug cycle costs the whole chain.

The one-line summary: **`serial` is a correct fix for tests that are already dependent, not a
licence to write dependent tests.**

## The real answer: log in once, reuse the state

Playwright can save a logged-in session to a file and hand it to every test. Each test still
gets its own isolated context — it just starts with the cookies already in place.

```ts
// One setup project runs first and saves the session
await page.context().storageState({ path: "playwright/.auth/leela.json" });

// Every other test starts from it
test.use({ storageState: "playwright/.auth/leela.json" });
```

| | Shared page (`beforeAll`) | Saved storage state |
|---|---|---|
| Logins performed | 1 | 1 |
| Tests independent? | **no** | **yes** |
| Can run in parallel? | no | yes |
| Can run one alone? | no | yes |
| Failure cascades? | yes | no |

Same saving, none of the costs. This is what production suites do, and it is Week 7 material in
this course — worth knowing now so you recognise `beforeAll` login as a stepping stone rather
than the destination.

> **Honest caveat about this app.** `storageState` works by saving cookies and `localStorage`.
> The banking app keeps **neither** — Day 2.2 Example 1 showed both are empty even when signed
> in, because its login is in-memory only. So on *this* app `storageState` would save an empty
> file and change nothing. The pattern is still the right answer for real applications, which is
> why it's here; just don't expect it to help you on this one.

**Expected:** five lines mapping situation to tool.

The last row is the one that catches people. "Test B needs what test A made" feels like a
dependency, but it usually isn't: B can create its own booking, order or payee via a helper or
an API call in a fraction of the time, and then it runs alone, in parallel, in any order.

Reach for a real dependency only when the *sequence itself* is what you're testing.

## What a reviewer checks

- **Is `serial` load-bearing, or a workaround?** If the tests could each make their own data, they should.
- **Can every test run alone?** `npx playwright test -g "Step 3"` should pass by itself.
- **Is `workers: 1` set globally** to fix a local problem? That's a suite-wide tax.
- **Is anything opened in `beforeAll` closed in `afterAll`?**
- **Is a login repeated 50 times** where `storageState` would do it once?

**Next:** [Day 2.4](/learn/w3/d2/p4) — your turn.

# Week 3, Day 2.4 — Practice

Three problems. No answer key.

App: `https://test-automation-banking.vercel.app/`. Tiles verified to exist:
`Transaction History` → `accountDashboard`, `Pay Bills` → `paymentDashboard`,
`Add Payee` → `transferDashboard`, plus `Manage Payee`, `Recharge`, `Billing History`,
`My Transactions`.

> Stuck past twenty minutes? Back to [Day 2.1](/learn/w3/d2/p1) or [Day 2.2](/learn/w3/d2/p2).

## When you're done

**Run one of your Problem 3 tests on its own.** If it passes, you've built the property that
matters most in CI: a failure you can reproduce in isolation. That single ability saves more
time than every timeout tweak in Day 1 combined.

**Next:** [Day 3.1](/learn/w3/d3/p1) — moving the repeated login into one shared class.

problems.statement:
**Build.** Demonstrate isolation to a colleague who doesn't believe you.

1. A test that signs in and asserts it reached `/dashboard`
2. A **second** test that navigates straight to `/dashboard` and asserts it gets bounced to the
   login form
3. Both using the plain `page` fixture, no hooks

**Check yourself.** Both pass. If test 2 finds the dashboard, you shared state somewhere by
accident — find where.

> **Hint** — test 2 should assert on something only the login page has.

**Build.** The same journey twice, and time the difference.

Write two `describe` groups that each visit four dashboard tiles and assert the URL:

- **Group A** — `beforeEach` signs in fresh for every test
- **Group B** — `beforeAll` signs in once and shares the page (mark it `serial`)

**Check yourself.** Both groups pass, and Group B is measurably faster — report both numbers.
Then answer: how much of B's saving would survive if the suite ran on 4 workers?

> **Hint** — `--reporter=list` prints per-test durations. The answer to the worker question is
> not "all of it".

**Build.** Take a dependent chain and remove the dependency.

Start from this deliberately bad shape: four tests sharing one page via `beforeAll`, where each
depends on the one before (navigate to a tile, then act, then check history). Rewrite it so
every test is independent — each sets up what it needs and asserts on its own.

**Where.** A spec in `week3/generated/`.

**Constraints — these are the exercise:**

- The rewritten version has **no `serial`** and **no shared mutable page**
- Every test passes when run alone: `npx playwright test <file> -g "<test name>"`
- No `waitForTimeout`

Then write, in a comment: *what did independence cost, and was it worth it here?*

**Check yourself.** Run the whole file, then run each test individually — all pass both ways.
Then run with `--workers=4` and confirm it's still green.

> **Hint** — the honest answer to the cost question may be "it got slower". Say so if it did;
> a suite that's 20% slower and debuggable is usually the better trade.
